clue.text: Walk over ?Not without some heavy going

definitions.meaning: to walk over something is to crush it underfoot
describes stamping along with heavy, thudding steps

explanation.surface: A walkover victory, the clue protests, was not without some heavy going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walk over' looks like a walkover, an easy win; it is the plain act of treading on something.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are crushing with the feet: treading down grass or people, and tramping with heavy steps.

clue.text: Credit on return of watch

parts.note: on tick means on credit

indicators.note: return of says the following little word is turned round

parts.note: re means on, concerning

explanation.surface: A watch is bought on credit and then sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return of' turns RE into ER. TICK is British slang for credit, as in buying 'on tick'.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang for a pocket timepiece, from the noise it makes.

clue.text: It oft proclaims the man, said Polonius

definitions.text: It oft proclaims the man, said Polonius

parts.words: It oft proclaims the man, said Polonius
parts.note: Polonius advises his son in Hamlet that what a person wears often reveals his character

explanation.surface: A line quoted from Shakespeare's Hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: Polonius tells Laertes: 'the apparel oft proclaims the man', meaning dress reveals character.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothing, the outward dress by which Polonius says a man is often judged.

clue.text: Plan of activity for a light weight

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
a gramme is a very small unit of weight

explanation.surface: A schedule designed for a lightweight boxer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'light weight' suggests a boxing class; it is a gramme, a tiny unit of mass.
explanation.definitionFit: A planned schedule or series of events, as in a programme of works.

clue.text: Would the Rev Spooner employ sons of toil in its manufacture ?

annotationWithheld.why: Would the Rev Spooner employ sons of toil in its manufacture ? -- a cryptic definition: Spooner's swap turns 'sons of toil' into 'tons of soil', the clay of the pottery; no spoonerism builds the answer's letters, and the check refuses a cd for a clue naming Spooner
annotationWithheld.clue: Would the Rev Spooner employ sons of toil in its manufacture ?

clue.text: Flower mob returns having suffered no casualties

indicators.note: the turned word holds the next piece inside it, as a container having contents
the word mob comes back, so its letters are read right to left

parts.note: taken as written
the setter takes the word for what was not suffered: casualties in battle are an army's losses

explanation.surface: A crowd comes home unharmed from a fight, having lost nobody.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface boasts of no casualties, yet a battle's casualties are its losses, and that is exactly the word the wordplay puts inside the turned crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloom is a flower, especially on a fruit tree in spring.

clue.text: There's a word puzzle about this transport

definitions.text: There's a word puzzle about this transport

parts.words: There's a word puzzle about this transport
parts.note: put re, meaning about, in front of the vehicle and you have a picture puzzle of words and letters

explanation.surface: A crossword is set about a means of transport.
explanation.walkthrough: RE (about) followed by the vehicle spells REBUS, a word puzzle in pictures; the clue says the puzzle is 'about' the transport.
explanation.definitionFit: A public road vehicle carrying passengers on a set route.

clue.text: Beheading a cipher should supply: the answer

indicators.note: beheading cuts off the head, the first letter, of the word for cipher

parts.note: a cipher is a zero, a nought

explanation.surface: Decapitating a coded message is supposed to reveal the solution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cipher' suggests a code; it is the old sense, the figure zero.
explanation.definitionFit: As an auxiliary verb it expresses duty, as in 'you must or are obliged to'.

clue.text: Is lyrical about a victory achieved by the thrifty

indicators.note: about means the first piece goes round the next ones

parts.note: to sing is to be lyrical

explanation.surface: Someone rhapsodises about a victory that was won economically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is lyrical' looks like praise; it means SINGS, which goes round A and V.
explanation.definitionFit: Money put aside is what frugal people accumulate.

clue.text: Jack Point, though moping mum

parts.note: Jack Point is the jester in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Yeomen of the Guard, a professional joker even when glum and silent

explanation.surface: A man named Jack sulks in silence.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Point, the jester of The Yeomen of the Guard, sings 'I have a song to sing, O' about a jester and his maid; by trade he is a jolly fellow even when moping and mum (silent).
explanation.definitionFit: A jester or clown, whose trade is cheerfulness, though Point ends his opera heartbroken.

clue.text: They fully inspire the love of children

definitions.text: They fully inspire the love of children

parts.words: They fully inspire the love of children
parts.note: 'cupboard love' is affection shown only to get food; storage places full of treats inspire it in children

explanation.surface: Something, when well stocked, makes children affectionate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cupboard love' is a British idiom for affection put on to get something, as a child sweet-talks whoever holds the biscuit tin.
explanation.definitionFit: Kitchen storage stocked with sweets earns a child's self-interested affection, the idiom's 'love'.

clue.text: Liberal party needs no consideration

parts.note: a liberal (generous) party, meaning person, hands things over without asking any consideration, the lawyer's word for payment

explanation.surface: Britain's Liberal Party is dismissed as not worth thinking about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal party' reads as the political party; here liberal means generous and party means person, and 'consideration' is payment in return.
explanation.definitionFit: A generous person donates freely and expects nothing back in exchange.

clue.text: No — all right!

parts.note: the blank completes the reassurance 'no mistake, all right', and a mistake is exactly what is not right

explanation.surface: Someone checks a sum and declares it correct.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash is a blank to fill: the stock phrase is 'no error', said when something checks out.
explanation.definitionFit: A mistake is the thing absent when everything checks out correct.

clue.text: Yet, chains somehow may lead to one getting lost

definitions.text: may lead to one getting lost

indicators.note: somehow says the letters of the two words get into place by some unstated rearrangement

parts.note: fodder taken as written
fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: Being chained up could, oddly, leave a person lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges the letters of YET and CHAINS. The definition leans on the proverb 'he who hesitates is lost'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says he who hesitates is lost, so wavering before acting brings loss.

clue.text: It perhaps, is a deep, soft hiding-place for diamonds

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters may be some other arrangement of themselves

parts.note: fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: Something is described as deep and soft, a good place to stash gems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges IS A DEEP SOFT. 'It' points ahead to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A secure bank box where valuables such as jewels are kept.

clue.text: Sinbad's Ancient Mariner?

parts.note: the creature in the Sinbad tale who rides on the sailor's shoulders, read word by word as aged, male and seafaring

explanation.surface: Coleridge's poem is imagined transplanted into the Arabian Nights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ancient Mariner' points at Coleridge, but Sinbad's tale has its own figure: ancient is OLD, mariner is MAN OF THE SEA.
explanation.definitionFit: In the fifth voyage of Sinbad, an elderly being clings to the sailor's back; its title literally means an aged seafarer.

clue.text: Music-maker's brief hour embracing a girl

indicators.note: embracing means the shortened hour holds the next letter inside

parts.note: hr is the short form of hour
Monica is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A musician spends a short hour hugging a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Music-maker' suggests a person, but it is the instrument; 'girl' is a plain girl's name, as old Times setters often used.
explanation.definitionFit: A mouth organ is a small instrument played by blowing and drawing breath.

clue.text: Prince's articles on fish

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the articles sit above the fish

parts.note: a and the are the indefinite and definite articles
ling is a sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: Royal items are placed on top of seafood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'articles' looks like possessions; it is grammar's A and THE.
explanation.definitionFit: An Anglo-Saxon nobleman or heir of royal blood.

clue.text: Outside left, outside right and centre-—selector's choice can make money

definitions.text: Outside left, outside right and centre-—selector's choice can make money

parts.words: Outside left, outside right and centre-—selector's choice can make money
parts.note: football positions disguise a con game: cards placed left, right and centre, the punter picks one, and the dealer profits

explanation.surface: A football selector chooses his wingers and centre forward and hopes it pays.
explanation.walkthrough: Outside left and outside right are old football positions, but here they are three playing cards laid out; the punter bets on which one is the queen, and only the dealer makes money.
explanation.definitionFit: A street swindle in which punters guess the queen among three shuffled cards and nearly always lose.

clue.text: Little Latin 'queen is only finishing a course

parts.note: R abbreviates regina, Latin for queen
taken as written
sole means only

explanation.surface: A small queen in Latin class is the only one completing her studies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'course' suggests study; it is a course of a meal. 'finishing' joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A fried cake of minced meat or fish, served as one dish of a meal.

clue.text: Hypocrisy at a musical performance

parts.note: cant is hypocritical, sanctimonious talk
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone notices insincerity at a concert.
explanation.definitionFit: A choral work for voices and orchestra, sung rather than staged.

clue.text: Classes for waitresses and clergymen

definitions.meaning: ranks or categories, as in the lower ranks of society
waitresses take diners' requests and clergymen take holy ones, both called by one word

explanation.surface: Lessons are being run for waitresses and priests.
explanation.walkthrough: Clergymen 'take holy orders' when ordained; waitresses take customers' requests for food.
explanation.definitionFit: Ranks of society, food requests to a waitress, and the holy ordination of clergy all share one word.

clue.text: City's way of implying the West End's expensive

definitions.text: City's way of implying the West End's expensive

parts.words: City's way of implying the West End's expensive
parts.note: a street in the City of London whose name, read as a compass point plus 'inexpensive', suggests the opposite end is dear

explanation.surface: City workers sneer that the West End is overpriced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City' is the City of London, the financial district; 'way' is a street. If the east is cheap, the west must be dear, i.e. expensive.
explanation.definitionFit: A street in the City of London's financial district, named for an old market; split up, it says east is inexpensive.

clue.text: Reconnoitred by burglars in the fourth instance, literally

parts.note: a case is an instance
D is the fourth letter of the alphabet, taken literally as a letter

explanation.surface: A building was scouted by burglars on the fourth occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'literally' says take 'the fourth' as a letter, D, so 'the fourth instance' is case D, as in cases A, B, C, D.
explanation.definitionFit: Criminal slang for inspecting a place in advance before robbing it.

clue.text: Has he got the lot or about three quarters ?

indicators.note: about means the two letters of or go round the other piece

parts.note: taken as written
the quarters are the compass points; three of them are west, north and east

explanation.surface: A gambler wonders whether he has won everything or only seventy-five per cent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'three quarters' looks like 75 per cent; the quarters are the four compass points, of which W, N and E are taken. A lot is a plot of land or an item at auction.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone holding title to a lot, as in property or an auction item, is its proprietor.

clue.text: In France they embrace the same false notions

indicators.note: embrace means the first piece wraps its arms around the second

parts.note: ils is French for they
do, short for ditto, means the same again

explanation.surface: The French are accused of clinging to identical misconceptions.
explanation.walkthrough: DO (ditto) is the abbreviation used in lists for 'the same'. Francis Bacon called deep-rooted false notions 'idols'.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon named humanity's habitual errors of thought the idols of the tribe, cave, market and theatre.

clue.text: Gum tree consumed (chew well)

parts.note: mastic is a resin gum and the Mediterranean tree that yields it
ate means consumed

explanation.surface: A eucalyptus has been eaten, with advice to chew it thoroughly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gum tree' suggests a eucalyptus; it is mastic, both a resin and the tree that gives it.
explanation.definitionFit: To grind food thoroughly with the teeth before swallowing.

clue.text: Every one called Jack

parts.note: the idiom 'every ... jack' means every single one, so every one is a fellow addressed as Jack

explanation.surface: Everyone with a particular first name is summoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' as a form of address means a man in general, and 'every man jack' means every single person.
explanation.definitionFit: A male person; any fellow may be hailed as Jack.

clue.text: Undergo torture for reward.

indicators.note: torture twists the word undergo out of shape into a new order

parts.note: fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is told to endure pain in return for a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'torture' rearranges the letters of UNDERGO.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic, poetic word for a recompense or prize.

clue.text: Brewer's assistants foil certain fortune-tellers

parts.note: small sachets help someone brewing a cuppa, and because they keep the leaves inside they defeat readers of leaves in the cup

explanation.surface: A brewery's staff thwart some clairvoyants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brewer' suggests beer; here it is someone making tea. Fortune-tellers who read tea leaves have nothing to read when the leaves stay in a sachet.
explanation.definitionFit: Porous paper pouches of tea that infuse in the pot, leaving no loose leaves behind.
